VIDEO.title: Matthew 10:34-42 – Why Did Jesus Say He's Bringing a SWORD?
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: I will wait for the God of my salvation.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 10:34-42, the end of Jesus' mission discourse (the second of Matthew's five). Jesus says He came to bring not peace but a sword, setting family members against each other; whoever loves family more than Him, or will not take up his cross, is not worthy of Him. Then the focus shifts to those who receive the disciples: even a cup of cold water will be rewarded.

Isn't Jesus the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who came to proclaim release and good news (Luke 4:18-19)? Luke's parallel even says 'hate' father and mother (Luke 14:26), a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Putting the rabbi before one's father was not new: the Mishnah tells a student to help his teacher first, 'as his father brought him into this world, and his teacher… brings him to life in the World-to-Come.'

The key is a remez, a hint that calls a whole Old Testament passage to mind. Jesus' list of family members comes from Micah 7:6. Micah indicts Israel's corrupt leaders and false prophets (Micah 3), calls for justice, lovingkindness and humility (Micah 6:8), and warns that what they try to keep will be given 'to the sword' (Micah 6:14).

Micah 7:6 is followed by hope: 'But as for me, I will watch expectantly for Yahweh… My God will hear me' (Micah 7:7). Micah also promises the ruler from Bethlehem who will shepherd His flock, 'And this One will be peace' (Micah 5:2-5), a passage Matthew already quoted (2:6). Jesus brings that peace, and it divides the corrupt from those who obey God.

Micah speaks of 'the remnant of Jacob' among many peoples (Micah 5:7-8) and of God who forgives 'the remnant of His inheritance' (Micah 7:18). The disciples may have expected all Israel to be redeemed and the Romans driven out; Jesus tempers their expectations.

The lesson for the original audience: it is in the midst of wicked people that God's remnant is found. Do not be surprised or discouraged when the gospel divides; trust that the Lord hears you, and keep looking for those who will receive the message.
QUOTES: Jesus is not introducing a new concept. He's reinforcing an established concept.
These statements act as a hint.
It is in the midst of wicked people that God's remnant is found.
They should not be discouraged when the gospel brings division.
The Lord's plan of redemption was and still is to seek his remnant among the peoples.

method.p: The teacher's tip: when Jesus drops a phrase from the Old Testament, like a hyperlink into the Tanakh, go and read the whole passage it comes from. The hint is meant to bring disciples back to the fuller message, including the verse right after it.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Do not think that I came to bring peace on the earth; I did not come to bring peace, but a sword.
For son treats father as a wicked fool; / Daughter rises up against her mother, / Daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; / A man’s enemies are the men of his own household.
But as for me, I will watch expectantly for Yahweh; / I will wait for the God of my salvation. / My God will hear me.

src.text: “Do not think that I came to bring peace on the earth; I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be the members of his household.

lines.text: These verses close the mission discourse. Jesus keeps preparing the disciples for what they will meet when they take the gospel out.
Note the list of family members: man and father, daughter and mother, daughter-in-law and mother-in-law. The teacher says to remember it; it is the key.
Luke's parallel says 'division' instead of 'a sword' (Luke 12:51-53).

left.text: For a child will be born to us, a son will be given to us; / And the government will rest on His shoulders; / And His name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, / Eternal Father, Prince of Peace.

right.text: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, / Because He anointed Me to preach the gospel to the poor. / He has sent Me to proclaim release to the captives, / And recovery of sight to the blind, / To set free those who are oppressed,

lines.text: Isaiah calls the Messiah the Prince of Peace, and in Luke 4 Jesus reads Isaiah 61 about release and good news. So is Jesus contradicting Himself when He says He will divide families? Or is something else going on?
Jesus also says, 'My peace I give to you; not as the world gives' (John 14:27).

src.text: “He who loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me; and he who loves son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me. And he who does not take his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me. He who has found his life will lose it, and he who has lost his life for My sake will find it.

lines.text: Luke's version uses 'hate' (Luke 14:26). In Hebrew idiom 'hate' can mean 'love less'; Matthew spells out the meaning: love Jesus more than family.
This is the first time Matthew mentions a cross; Jesus repeats the call in 16:24-25.

src.text: “He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives Him who sent Me. He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward. And whoever in the name of a disciple gives to one of these little ones even a cup of cold water to drink, truly I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.”

lines.text: The focus shifts from the disciples to those who receive their message. The promise sounds like John 6:37-39: Jesus will lose nothing of all the Father has given Him.
'Little ones' are Jesus' disciples (18:6); He says the same about receiving His messengers in John 13:20.

Putting one's rabbi before one's father was not new. The Mishnah: if a student's father and teacher are both in captivity, 'he first redeems his teacher and thereafter redeems his father' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11).

Likewise if both are carrying burdens: 'he first places his teacher's burden down and thereafter places his father's burden down' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11). Jesus is reinforcing an established idea, not inventing one.
The same passage makes an exception: if the father is himself a Torah scholar, the father comes first.

left.text: He who has found his life will lose it, and he who has lost his life for My sake will find it.

lines.text: Verse 39 fits another line in the same Mishnah: the teacher comes first 'as his father brought him into this world, and his teacher, who taught him the wisdom of Torah, brings him to life in the World-to-Come' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11).
The Mishnah was written down about AD 200, so it shows later rabbinic teaching; it is a window on the world of rabbis and students, not a source Jesus quoted.

A remez is a call back to the Old Testament, like a hyperlink to something in the Tanakh. Jesus does not quote a whole chapter; He drops a phrase, and the hint brings His students back to the passage so they can reflect on God's word.
Jesus' students could understand Him more deeply in the moment if they knew their text. In 10:34-37 the hint points to the prophet Micah.

left.text: And I said, / “Hear now, heads of Jacob / And rulers of the house of Israel. / Is it not for you to know justice?

right.text: He has told you, O man, what is good; / And what does Yahweh require of you / But to do justice, to love lovingkindness, / And to walk humbly with your God?

lines.text: Micah's message: stop breaking the covenant, flee corruption, care for the poor and oppressed. He calls out the leaders in words that sound like Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, and the prophets who cry 'Peace' when they are fed (Micah 3:5).
God would strike them and make them desolate because of their sins; what they tried to keep, 'I will give to the sword' (Micah 6:14).

REMNANT.title: A man's enemies, and a God who hears

src.text: For son treats father as a wicked fool; / Daughter rises up against her mother, / Daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; / A man’s enemies are the men of his own household. But as for me, I will watch expectantly for Yahweh; / I will wait for the God of my salvation. / My God will hear me.

lines.text: Jesus' list follows Micah 7:6. The video's reading: the corruption Micah described is present among them, and Jesus' teaching will bring a sword to all the corrupt try to keep, dividing those who obey God from those who do not.
When the disciples heard the hint, they should have remembered 7:6 and then 7:7: in the midst of strife, disciples can look to the Lord, trust Him, and know He will hear them.

REMNANT.title: And this One will be peace

src.text: But as for you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, / Too little to be among the clans of Judah, / From you One will go forth for Me to be ruler in Israel. / His goings forth are from everlasting, / From the ancient days.”

right.text: And He will stand and shepherd His flock / In the strength of Yahweh, / In the majesty of the name of Yahweh His God. / And they will remain / Because at that time He will be great / To the ends of the earth. And this One will be peace.

lines.text: Jesus says 'I came to,' then alludes to Micah 7. Micah's events had already happened in some sense, and in some sense not yet: Micah also looks ahead to the Messiah. Matthew quoted Micah 5:2 at Jesus' birth (2:6).
So Jesus came to be the shepherd who 'will be peace,' and that coming stirs up division among those who refuse to repent.

left.text: Then the remnant of Jacob / Will be among many peoples / Like dew from Yahweh, / Like showers on vegetation / Which do not hope for man / Or wait for the sons of men.

right.text: Who is a God like You, who forgives iniquity / And passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance? / He does not hold fast to His anger forever / Because He delights in lovingkindness.

lines.text: God will forgive, but the promise is for the remnant. The disciples likely expected the whole nation to be redeemed and a military Messiah to beat Rome. The Lord's plan was, and is, to seek His remnant among the peoples.
So the disciples should not be surprised when not everyone welcomes them, nor discouraged when the gospel divides. They look for those who receive them (10:40-42), as Acts shows.

TERMS.def: A 'hint': a short phrase that calls a whole Old Testament passage to mind. The captions hear it as 'Rome' and 'Rams.'
Hebrew for a disciple or student of a rabbi.
The first written collection of rabbinic oral law, compiled about AD 200.
Rabbinic phrase (olam ha-ba) for the life of the age to come.
The faithful part of God's people whom He preserves and forgives (Micah 5:7-8; 7:18).
One of the Messiah's names in Isaiah 9:6.
Accept shame and death for Jesus' sake, as a condemned man carried his cross to execution.
Jesus' name for His humble disciples (10:42; 18:6, 10, 14).

WORDS.gloss: Sword, a short sword or long knife. Look up: BDAG, μάχαιρα.
To divide in two, set at variance.
Remnant, what is left. Look up: BDB or HALOT, שְׁאֵרִית.
To treat as a fool, with contempt.

BACKGROUND.p: In the first century, family was a person's identity, livelihood and security. Following a rabbi whom one's family rejected could cost all three.

Later rabbinic teaching ranked the teacher above the father in some duties: 'his father brought him into this world, and his teacher, who taught him the wisdom of Torah, brings him to life in the World-to-Come' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11).
Micah prophesied in the late 700s BC, when Assyria destroyed Samaria (722 BC) and threatened Jerusalem. He was a contemporary of Isaiah.
Many Jews hoped for an anointed king who would defeat Rome and restore Israel's independence; some rebels in the first century claimed that role. Jesus' kingdom came another way.

DEBATES.p: Both are true: Jesus brings peace with God (Micah 5:5; John 14:27), but His coming divides those who receive Him from those who refuse. The sword is the result, not the goal; Chrysostom: 'the war is not then the effect of His purpose.'
The video: in some sense yes, in Micah's day, and in some sense not yet; the pattern returns when the Messiah comes. Others read Jesus as using Micah's words as a pattern rather than a prediction.
Luke 14:26 says 'hate'; Matthew 10:37 says 'loves… more than Me.' Most read Luke's word as a Semitic idiom for preferring one over another (compare Genesis 29:30-31).

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video reads Micah 5:2-5 as one verse ('Micah 5 verse 2'); 'And this One will be peace' is 5:5 in the LSB.
Micah 3:5 condemns prophets who cry 'Peace' when fed and declare war on those who do not feed them; it does not speak of caring for outcasts.
On 'hate': Luke keeps the Hebrew idiom ('hate' meaning 'love less'), and Matthew gives its sense ('loves… more than Me'), so it is Luke, not Matthew, that preserves the idiom.

The Mishnah sayings are real (Bava Metzia 2:11), but the Mishnah was compiled about AD 200, so they show later rabbinic practice. The passage also adds an exception when the father is a Torah scholar.

QUESTIONS: How can Jesus be the Prince of Peace and bring a sword? How would you explain it to a friend?
Has following Jesus ever caused tension in your family? How did you respond?
Read Micah 7:5-7. How does verse 7 change the way you hear Matthew 10:35-36?
What does 'take his cross and follow after Me' look like in your week?
Who are the 'little ones' around you who could use a cup of cold water?
Where might God's remnant be waiting among people you assume would never listen?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: it is in the midst of wicked people that God's remnant is found. The disciples probably believed the whole nation of Israel would be redeemed, and many expected a military Messiah who would defeat the Romans. But the Lord's plan of redemption, then and now, is to seek His remnant among the peoples. Jesus spoke these things to temper their expectations and prepare them for reality: not everyone would welcome them. Among people who would refuse and even harm them, they were to look for those who would receive them (10:40-42), and that is what Acts shows. They should not be surprised or discouraged when the gospel brings division; they should remember Micah 7:6-7 and trust that the Lord hears them and will guide them to His remnant. Does that still preach today? Are you, and is your church, seeking God's remnant among the wicked?
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): read Micah 7:1-20 in one sitting this week. Then write the name of one person you have given up on, and pray Micah 7:7 and 7:18 for them each day.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 10:34-42, the end of Jesus' mission discourse (the second of Matthew's five). Jesus says He came to bring not peace but a sword, setting family members against each other; whoever loves family more than Him, or will not take up his cross, is not worthy of Him. Then the focus shifts to those who receive the disciples: even a cup of cold water will be rewarded.
- Isn't Jesus the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who came to proclaim release and good news (Luke 4:18-19)? Luke's parallel even says 'hate' father and mother (Luke 14:26), a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Putting the rabbi before one's father was not new: the Mishnah tells a student to help his teacher first, 'as his father brought him into this world, and his teacher… brings him to life in the World-to-Come.'
- The key is a remez, a hint that calls a whole Old Testament passage to mind. Jesus' list of family members comes from Micah 7:6. Micah indicts Israel's corrupt leaders and false prophets (Micah 3), calls for justice, lovingkindness and humility (Micah 6:8), and warns that what they try to keep will be given 'to the sword' (Micah 6:14).
- Micah 7:6 is followed by hope: 'But as for me, I will watch expectantly for Yahweh… My God will hear me' (Micah 7:7). Micah also promises the ruler from Bethlehem who will shepherd His flock, 'And this One will be peace' (Micah 5:2-5), a passage Matthew already quoted (2:6). Jesus brings that peace, and it divides the corrupt from those who obey God.
- Micah speaks of 'the remnant of Jacob' among many peoples (Micah 5:7-8) and of God who forgives 'the remnant of His inheritance' (Micah 7:18). The disciples may have expected all Israel to be redeemed and the Romans driven out; Jesus tempers their expectations.
- The lesson for the original audience: it is in the midst of wicked people that God's remnant is found. Do not be surprised or discouraged when the gospel divides; trust that the Lord hears you, and keep looking for those who will receive the message.

2. A contradiction?: The Prince of Peace

   (video) Isaiah calls the Messiah the Prince of Peace, and in Luke 4 Jesus reads Isaiah 61 about release and good news. So is Jesus contradicting Himself when He says He will divide families? Or is something else going on?
   [Background] Jesus also says, 'My peace I give to you; not as the world gives' (John 14:27). (John 14:27)
3. Matthew 10:37-39: Take his cross and follow
   Worthy Matthew 10:37-39: "“He who loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me; and he who loves son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me. And he who does not take his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me. He who has found his life will lose it, and he who has lost his life for My sake will find it." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:37-39
   (video) Luke's version uses 'hate' (Luke 14:26). In Hebrew idiom 'hate' can mean 'love less'; Matthew spells out the meaning: love Jesus more than family. (Luke 14:26-27)
   [Background] This is the first time Matthew mentions a cross; Jesus repeats the call in 16:24-25. (Matthew 16:24-25)
4. Matthew 10:40-42: A cup of cold water
   Reward Matthew 10:40-42: "“He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives Him who sent Me. He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward. And whoever in the name of a disciple gives to one of these little ones even a cup of cold water to drink, truly I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:40-42
   (video) The focus shifts from the disciples to those who receive their message. The promise sounds like John 6:37-39: Jesus will lose nothing of all the Father has given Him. (John 6:37-39)
   [Background] 'Little ones' are Jesus' disciples (18:6); He says the same about receiving His messengers in John 13:20. (Matthew 18:6; John 13:20)

## The rabbi before the father
1. Rabbi and talmid: Your teacher first
   (video) Putting one's rabbi before one's father was not new. The Mishnah: if a student's father and teacher are both in captivity, 'he first redeems his teacher and thereafter redeems his father' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11).
   (video) Likewise if both are carrying burdens: 'he first places his teacher's burden down and thereafter places his father's burden down' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11). Jesus is reinforcing an established idea, not inventing one.
   [Background] The same passage makes an exception: if the father is himself a Torah scholar, the father comes first.
2. Matthew 10:39: Life in the World-to-Come
   Jesus (Matthew 10:39, LSB): "He who has found his life will lose it, and he who has lost his life for My sake will find it."
   (video) Verse 39 fits another line in the same Mishnah: the teacher comes first 'as his father brought him into this world, and his teacher, who taught him the wisdom of Torah, brings him to life in the World-to-Come' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11).
   [Background] The Mishnah was written down about AD 200, so it shows later rabbinic teaching; it is a window on the world of rabbis and students, not a source Jesus quoted.
3. How Jesus teaches: A hint to the Tanakh
   (video) A remez is a call back to the Old Testament, like a hyperlink to something in the Tanakh. Jesus does not quote a whole chapter; He drops a phrase, and the hint brings His students back to the passage so they can reflect on God's word.
   (video) Jesus' students could understand Him more deeply in the moment if they knew their text. In 10:34-37 the hint points to the prophet Micah.

## Micah and the remnant
1. Micah 3 and 6: Corruption in Micah's day
   Micah (Micah 3:1, LSB): "And I said, / “Hear now, heads of Jacob / And rulers of the house of Israel. / Is it not for you to know justice?"
   Micah (Micah 6:8, LSB): "He has told you, O man, what is good; / And what does Yahweh require of you / But to do justice, to love lovingkindness, / And to walk humbly with your God?"
   (video) Micah's message: stop breaking the covenant, flee corruption, care for the poor and oppressed. He calls out the leaders in words that sound like Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, and the prophets who cry 'Peace' when they are fed (Micah 3:5). (Micah 3:5)
   (video) God would strike them and make them desolate because of their sins; what they tried to keep, 'I will give to the sword' (Micah 6:14). (Micah 6:13-14)
2. Micah 7:5-7: A man's enemies, and a God who hears
   Hope Micah 7:6-7: "For son treats father as a wicked fool; / Daughter rises up against her mother, / Daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; / A man’s enemies are the men of his own household. But as for me, I will watch expectantly for Yahweh; / I will wait for the God of my salvation. / My God will hear me." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Micah+7:6-7
   (video) Jesus' list follows Micah 7:6. The video's reading: the corruption Micah described is present among them, and Jesus' teaching will bring a sword to all the corrupt try to keep, dividing those who obey God from those who do not.
   (video) When the disciples heard the hint, they should have remembered 7:6 and then 7:7: in the midst of strife, disciples can look to the Lord, trust Him, and know He will hear them.
3. Micah 5:2-5: And this One will be peace
   Micah (Micah 5:4-5, LSB): "And He will stand and shepherd His flock / In the strength of Yahweh, / In the majesty of the name of Yahweh His God. / And they will remain / Because at that time He will be great / To the ends of the earth. And this One will be peace."
   Messiah Micah 5:2: "But as for you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, / Too little to be among the clans of Judah, / From you One will go forth for Me to be ruler in Israel. / His goings forth are from everlasting, / From the ancient days.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Micah+5:2
   (video) Jesus says 'I came to,' then alludes to Micah 7. Micah's events had already happened in some sense, and in some sense not yet: Micah also looks ahead to the Messiah. Matthew quoted Micah 5:2 at Jesus' birth (2:6). (Matthew 2:6)
   (video) So Jesus came to be the shepherd who 'will be peace,' and that coming stirs up division among those who refuse to repent.
4. Micah 5:7 and 7:18: The remnant of His inheritance
   Micah (Micah 5:7, LSB): "Then the remnant of Jacob / Will be among many peoples / Like dew from Yahweh, / Like showers on vegetation / Which do not hope for man / Or wait for the sons of men."
   Micah (Micah 7:18, LSB): "Who is a God like You, who forgives iniquity / And passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance? / He does not hold fast to His anger forever / Because He delights in lovingkindness."
   (video) God will forgive, but the promise is for the remnant. The disciples likely expected the whole nation to be redeemed and a military Messiah to beat Rome. The Lord's plan was, and is, to seek His remnant among the peoples.
   (video) So the disciples should not be surprised when not everyone welcomes them, nor discouraged when the gospel divides. They look for those who receive them (10:40-42), as Acts shows.

## Key people
- Jesus: Brings a sword that divides, and the peace Micah promised. [Background] This is the end of the second discourse; 11:1 closes it: 'when Jesus had finished giving instructions.'
- The Twelve: Must love Jesus more than family and take up their cross. [Background] Peter later says, 'we have left everything and followed You' (19:27).
- Those who receive them: Even a cup of cold water to a disciple will be rewarded. [Background] Compare Matthew 25:35-40: 'I was thirsty, and you gave Me something to drink.'
- Micah: The prophet behind Jesus' words in 10:35-36. [Background] From Moresheth, he prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah (Micah 1:1).
- Heads of Jacob and the false prophets: Israel's corrupt leaders in Micah's day. [Background] Jeremiah 26:18 recalls Micah's warning that Zion would be plowed like a field.
- The remnant: Those God saves from among the wicked. [Background] Paul: 'at the present time a remnant according to the choice of grace has come to be' (Romans 11:5).

## Places [Background]
- Bethlehem (named in the video): Micah 5:2: the ruler who 'will be peace' comes from Bethlehem Ephrathah (quoted in Matthew 2:6).
- Jerusalem: Micah warned its rulers that Zion would be plowed like a field (Micah 3:12).
- Samaria: Capital of the northern kingdom; Micah's vision concerned 'Samaria and Jerusalem' (Micah 1:1).
- Capernaum: Where Jesus likely spoke to the Twelve before sending them.

## Key terms
- Remez: A 'hint': a short phrase that calls a whole Old Testament passage to mind. The captions hear it as 'Rome' and 'Rams.'
- Talmid: Hebrew for a disciple or student of a rabbi.
- Mishnah: The first written collection of rabbinic oral law, compiled about AD 200.
- World-to-Come: Rabbinic phrase (olam ha-ba) for the life of the age to come.
- Remnant: The faithful part of God's people whom He preserves and forgives (Micah 5:7-8; 7:18).
- Prince of Peace: One of the Messiah's names in Isaiah 9:6.
- Take up the cross: Accept shame and death for Jesus' sake, as a condemned man carried his cross to execution. [Background]
- Little ones: Jesus' name for His humble disciples (10:42; 18:6, 10, 14). [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Family and honor: In the first century, family was a person's identity, livelihood and security. Following a rabbi whom one's family rejected could cost all three.
- Rabbi before father: Later rabbinic teaching ranked the teacher above the father in some duties: 'his father brought him into this world, and his teacher, who taught him the wisdom of Torah, brings him to life in the World-to-Come' (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:11).
- Micah's world: Micah prophesied in the late 700s BC, when Assyria destroyed Samaria (722 BC) and threatened Jerusalem. He was a contemporary of Isaiah.
- Expecting a Messiah: Many Jews hoped for an anointed king who would defeat Rome and restore Israel's independence; some rebels in the first century claimed that role. Jesus' kingdom came another way.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Because this more than anything is peace, when the diseased is cut off, when the mutinous is removed." Homilies on Matthew 35, on 10:34. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "The war is not then the effect of His purpose, but of their temper." Homilies on Matthew 35, on 10:34. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Though a cup of cold water be your gift, on which there is nothing laid out, even of this shall a reward be stored up for you." Homilies on Matthew 35, on 10:42. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Sword or peace? Both are true: Jesus brings peace with God (Micah 5:5; John 14:27), but His coming divides those who receive Him from those who refuse. The sword is the result, not the goal; Chrysostom: 'the war is not then the effect of His purpose.'
- Has Micah 7 already happened? The video: in some sense yes, in Micah's day, and in some sense not yet; the pattern returns when the Messiah comes. Others read Jesus as using Micah's words as a pattern rather than a prediction.
- 'Hate' or 'love more'? Luke 14:26 says 'hate'; Matthew 10:37 says 'loves… more than Me.' Most read Luke's word as a Semitic idiom for preferring one over another (compare Genesis 29:30-31).

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video reads Micah 5:2-5 as one verse ('Micah 5 verse 2'); 'And this One will be peace' is 5:5 in the LSB.
- Micah 3:5 condemns prophets who cry 'Peace' when fed and declare war on those who do not feed them; it does not speak of caring for outcasts.
- On 'hate': Luke keeps the Hebrew idiom ('hate' meaning 'love less'), and Matthew gives its sense ('loves… more than Me'), so it is Luke, not Matthew, that preserves the idiom.
- The Mishnah sayings are real (Bava Metzia 2:11), but the Mishnah was compiled about AD 200, so they show later rabbinic practice. The passage also adds an exception when the father is a Torah scholar.
- The captions hear 'remez' as 'Rome' and 'Rams.'

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. How can Jesus be the Prince of Peace and bring a sword? How would you explain it to a friend?
2. Has following Jesus ever caused tension in your family? How did you respond?
3. Read Micah 7:5-7. How does verse 7 change the way you hear Matthew 10:35-36?
4. What does 'take his cross and follow after Me' look like in your week?
5. Who are the 'little ones' around you who could use a cup of cold water?
6. Where might God's remnant be waiting among people you assume would never listen?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: it is in the midst of wicked people that God's remnant is found. The disciples probably believed the whole nation of Israel would be redeemed, and many expected a military Messiah who would defeat the Romans. But the Lord's plan of redemption, then and now, is to seek His remnant among the peoples. Jesus spoke these things to temper their expectations and prepare them for reality: not everyone would welcome them. Among people who would refuse and even harm them, they were to look for those who would receive them (10:40-42), and that is what Acts shows. They should not be surprised or discouraged when the gospel brings division; they should remember Micah 7:6-7 and trust that the Lord hears them and will guide them to His remnant. Does that still preach today? Are you, and is your church, seeking God's remnant among the wicked?
- Study note (added): read Micah 7:1-20 in one sitting this week. Then write the name of one person you have given up on, and pray Micah 7:7 and 7:18 for them each day.
